A dynasty that ruled the northern Tamil country and parts of the Deccan from 275 to 897, from their capital at Kanchipuram. Their script and temple style travelled across the sea to Southeast Asia.

The Pallavas first appear as governors under the Satavahanas and rose after that dynasty collapsed. They became a major power in the 7th century:

  • Mahendravarman I (about 600 to 630) wrote a Sanskrit comedy and began cutting temples from solid rock.
  • Narasimhavarman I (about 630 to 668), called Mamalla, "great wrestler", defeated the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II and sacked his capital Vatapi in 642.
  • Narasimhavarman II (about 700 to 728) built the Shore Temple and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram.

Their port of Mamallapuram, named after Mamalla, holds their best-known works: five temples carved as chariots from single boulders, a huge relief of the Descent of the Ganges, and the Shore Temple facing the Bay of Bengal. Together they mark the move in south India from rock-cut to free-standing stone temples.

Kanchipuram was a centre of learning in Sanskrit and Tamil, for Hindus, Buddhists and Jains. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited around 640. The Tamil Shaiva and Vaishnava poet-saints were active in these centuries.

The Pallavas looked to the sea. Their form of the south Indian Grantha script was taken up in Southeast Asia and grew into the scripts of Cambodia, Java and other lands, including the Khmer script. Their power ended in 897, when the rising Cholas defeated the last important Pallava king.
sum: A dynasty that ruled the northern Tamil country and parts of the Deccan from 275 to 897, from their capital at Kanchipuram. Their script and temple style travelled across the sea to Southeast Asia.
